//| echo: false
// Builds answer cards for any quiz on this page. Each card gives immediate feedback.
u5cCards = function(body, questions, onAnswer) {
  questions.forEach((qq, qi) => {
    const card = document.createElement("div");
    card.style.cssText = "background:#fff;color:#1e1b4b;border-radius:12px;padding:14px 16px;margin-bottom:12px;box-shadow:0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,.08);";
    const qp = document.createElement("p");
    qp.style.cssText = "font-weight:700;margin:0 0 8px;color:#1e1b4b;";
    qp.textContent = `${qi + 1}. ${qq.q}`;
    card.appendChild(qp);
    const fb = document.createElement("div");
    fb.setAttribute("aria-live", "polite");
    fb.style.cssText = "border-radius:8px;font-size:.92em;";
    const btns = qq.options.map((opt, oi) => {
      const btn = document.createElement("button");
      btn.type = "button";
      btn.textContent = opt;
      btn.style.cssText = "display:block;width:100%;min-height:44px;text-align:left;padding:10px 14px;margin:6px 0;border:2px solid #e2e8f0;border-radius:8px;background:#fff;color:#1e1b4b;cursor:pointer;font-size:.95em;";
      btn.onclick = () => {
        if (card.dataset.answered) return;
        card.dataset.answered = "true";
        btns.forEach(b => { b.style.cursor = "default"; b.style.color = "#475569"; });
        const right = btns[qq.correct];
        right.style.borderColor = "#16a34a"; right.style.background = "#f0fdf4"; right.style.color = "#14532d"; right.style.fontWeight = "700";
        const ok = oi === qq.correct;
        if (!ok) { btn.style.borderColor = "#dc2626"; btn.style.background = "#fef2f2"; btn.style.color = "#7f1d1d"; btn.style.fontWeight = "700"; }
        fb.textContent = (ok ? "✅ Correct! " : "❌ Not quite. ") + qq.explanation;
        fb.style.cssText = `border-radius:8px;font-size:.92em;padding:10px 14px;margin-top:8px;color:${ok ? "#14532d" : "#7f1d1d"};background:${ok ? "#f0fdf4" : "#fef2f2"};`;
        if (onAnswer) onAnswer(ok);
      };
      card.appendChild(btn);
      return btn;
    });
    card.appendChild(fb);
    body.appendChild(card);
  });
}
```

# Evidence Review: Revisiting the Performance Task {#u5c-evidence}

::: {.u5c-engage-box}
## 🧩 You broke "storm damage" into three subproblems

At the start of the unit you learned that storms cost the United States **billions of dollars** every year. Storm damage is too big to solve all at once, so you **broke it into smaller problems** and studied one in each lesson. At the end of each lesson, your PTO asked you to evaluate a solution and practice one **engineering component**. Review all three before you design.
:::

::: {.u5c-scroll}
| Lesson | Subproblem | Engineering component you practiced | Solution you evaluated |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Wind](unit5-wind.qmd) | Strong storm **winds** | **Identifying tradeoffs**: prioritize **criteria**, then decide if the benefits are worth the costs | Burying power lines; **wind farms** |
| [Water](unit5-water.qmd) | Heavy **precipitation** (rain and snow) | **Identifying constraints and limitations**: the limits a design must work within | **Solar geoengineering** (cooling the planet) |
| [Flooding](unit5-flooding.qmd) | **Coastal flooding** | **Design elements**: the parts you change, add or take away, each with **benefits** and **costs** | **Your own** flood design |
:::

::: {.u5c-key-idea}
### 🔑 Engineering words you'll use in your final design

- **Criteria**: what the design **needs to do** to succeed. The best criteria can be **measured** ("keeps water out of subway entrances during a storm tide as high as Sandy's").
- **Constraints**: **limits** on the design, like money, materials, space or time.
- **Limitations**: things the design **can't do**, even if it works perfectly.
- **Tradeoff**: giving up one thing to get another. Engineers decide if the **benefits are worth the costs**.
- **Design element**: one part of the solution, something you **change, add or take away** in the system.
- **Mechanism**: **how** the weather causes the damage. A strong solution acts on the mechanism, not just the damage.
:::

## Wind: Identifying Tradeoffs {#u5c-wind}

::: {.u5c-review}
### 💨 What you figured out about strong winds

- **Uneven heating** of Earth's surface makes some air warm and **less dense** (it rises, making **low pressure**) and some air cool and **more dense** (it sinks, making **high pressure**). **Wind** is air moving **from high to low pressure**.
- The same pattern works at every scale: the bottle model, molecules, and the global **convection cells**. With the **Coriolis effect** (a bend to the right in the Northern Hemisphere), the cells make the **wind belts**. NYC is in the **westerlies**, which carry storms **west to east**.
- **Winter Storm Jonas (January 22–24, 2016)** formed where cold, dense air from Canada met warm, moist air from the Gulf and Atlantic. A **big pressure difference over a short distance** made strong winds that spiraled **counterclockwise** into the low. Jonas dropped **27.5 in** of snow in Central Park, with gusts of **48 mph** at LaGuardia and JFK and **58–59 mph** on Long Island (National Weather Service).
- Storms follow **predictable paths**, so forecasters warned people days ahead. That's a **pattern** you can design with.

**Solutions you evaluated:**

- **Burying power lines** cuts outages from wind and falling trees, but costs much more (your packet estimates **5–10 times** the cost of overhead lines), and buried lines can flood and are harder to repair.
- **Wind farms**: turbines **lock and feather their blades** above **55 mph** to protect themselves (U.S. Department of Energy). **No real wind farm has been observed to weaken a storm.** That idea comes only from **computer models** of huge offshore arrays. Their proven benefit is **clean electricity**.

📖 Review: [Explaining the global movement of storms](unit5-wind.qmd#wd-explain-1) · [Explaining storm winds](unit5-wind.qmd#wd-explain-2) · [Mitigating hurricane winds](unit5-wind.qmd#wd-elaborate) · [Wind farms](unit5-wind.qmd#wd-evaluate) · [Your PTO page: Wind](unit5-wind.qmd#wd-pt)
:::

::: {.u5c-fix}
**📌 Packet note:** one Wind 5E question says Jonas "gusted up to 55 mph in New York City." The National Weather Service measured **48 mph** at LaGuardia and JFK; the 58–59 mph gusts were on **Long Island**. Also, the Evaluate question asks if wind farms reduce storm wind damage. Treat that as a **claim to test**: the storm-weakening idea is from models, not measurements.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!): Wind PTO, question 1 and 7

**Q1. How did Jonas's strong winds form, and how was the storm carried across the country?** Uneven heating made a cold, dense, high-pressure air mass (from Canada) and a warm, moist, low-pressure air mass (from the Gulf and Atlantic). Global winds brought them together, and where they met a low formed and deepened. Air rushed from high to low pressure, bent by the Coriolis effect into a counterclockwise spiral. The big pressure difference over a short distance made strong winds. The westerlies carried the storm east, then it turned north up the coast.

**Q7. Are the costs reasonable tradeoffs?** A strong answer **decides**, with reasons. Example: wind farms are worth it for **clean energy**, but not (yet) as a **storm-wind shield**, because turbines shut down in storm winds and the storm-weakening benefit has never been measured.
:::

## Water: Identifying Constraints and Limitations {#u5c-water}

::: {.u5c-review}
### 🌧️ What you figured out about heavy precipitation

- When a **warm, moist** air mass meets a **cold, dense** air mass at a **front**, the cold air pushes the warm air **up**. Rising air **cools**, and its water vapor **condenses** into clouds and precipitation. If the air it falls through is **at or below 32 °F (0 °C)**, it falls as **snow**.
- **Warm air can hold more water vapor**, about **7% more for every 1 °C** of warming (IPCC). That's why the warm, moist air from the Gulf and the warm Atlantic fed so much snow into Jonas.
- Precipitation follows **global patterns**: "wet" latitudes near **0° and 60°** (rising air) and "dry" latitudes near **30° and the poles** (sinking air).
- **Jonas:** **2.31 in** of liquid water fell in Central Park on January 23, 2016, as **27.3 in** of snow that day (NOAA). That's close to NYC's **29.8 in** average for a whole winter. **Hurricane Helene (2024)** dropped up to **30.78 in** of rain in the North Carolina mountains (National Hurricane Center).

**Solution you evaluated: solar geoengineering.** Reflect some sunlight back to space (with sulfur dioxide high in the atmosphere, or sea-salt spray that brightens clouds) so oceans stay cooler, less water evaporates, and storms carry less moisture.

- **Constraints** (limits on making it happen): the aircraft and spray equipment **don't exist yet**; it would take about **50 million metric tons** of sulfur dioxide a year by 2100 in NOAA's simulations; there are **no international rules** about who controls it.
- **Limitations** (what it can't do): it only **masks** warming and removes **no carbon dioxide**; one study found that cooling the ocean would weaken a hurricane by only about **15%** even in ideal conditions, and its title calls the idea **"futile."** Models also show side effects, such as **5–7% less rain** each year in parts of the tropics.

📖 Review: [Explaining precipitation formation](unit5-water.qmd#wt-explain) · [Precipitation in a changing climate](unit5-water.qmd#wt-elaborate) · [A potential solution to reduce precipitation](unit5-water.qmd#wt-evaluate) · [Your PTO page: Water](unit5-water.qmd#wt-pt)
:::

::: {.u5c-fix}
**📌 Packet note:** the Unit Plan says "cooling the oceans is the biggest thing that would reduce precipitation." The packet's own geoengineering text shows big limits (it only masks warming, the hardware doesn't exist, and the hurricane effect is small at best), so treat that as a **claim to evaluate**, not a fact. The Unit Plan also mentions **rain gardens**, but they aren't in the Water lesson. You may still use ideas like them in your design if you explain the mechanism.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!): Water PTO, questions 1 and 6

**Q1. How did Jonas's heavy precipitation form?** Warm, moist air from the Gulf of Mexico and the warm Atlantic was drawn north and forced **up over** cold, dense, dry air from Canada. The rising air cooled, water vapor **condensed** into thick clouds, and because the air was below 32 °F, it fell as heavy **snow**. Warm ocean water supplied extra moisture.

**Q6. Constraints and limitations.** *Constraints:* the hardware doesn't exist; it needs enormous yearly amounts of sulfur dioxide; it must run for decades without stopping; it needs global agreement with no rules in place; it costs money to fund. *Limitations:* it doesn't remove carbon dioxide or fix ocean acidification; its effect on hurricanes is small at best; nobody can control where the side effects land.
:::

## Flooding: Design Elements {#u5c-flooding}

::: {.u5c-review}
### 🌊 What you figured out about coastal flooding

- The Moon's gravity (and the Sun's) pulls the ocean into two **tidal bulges**, so NYC gets about **two high tides a day**.
- At **new and full moon**, the Sun and Moon pull along the **same line**: **spring tides**, with the highest highs. At the quarter moons they pull at **right angles**: **neap tides**. When a spring tide happens with the Moon near **perigee** (closest to Earth), you get the most extreme tides: **perigean spring tides**, or **king tides**.
- **Storm tide = tide + storm surge.** Storm winds and low pressure push extra water (the **surge**) onto the coast on top of the tide.
- **Hurricane Sandy:** on October 29, 2012, a **full moon**, Sandy's surge of about **9.3 ft** arrived near high tide. The water at The Battery reached a record **14.06 ft** above MLLW (the "zero" on tide charts), about **9 ft above an average high tide** (NOAA).
- **Sea-level rise** raises the starting point for every tide. Global sea level is up **8–9 in since 1880**, and U.S. **high-tide flooding** is **300% to more than 900%** more frequent than 50 years ago (NOAA Climate.gov).
- Tides are **predictable years ahead**. That's a **pattern** you can design with, like closing flood gates before a king tide plus a forecast surge.

📖 Review the [Flooding 5E](unit5-flooding.qmd): [Why Sandy and Marin flooded](unit5-flooding.qmd#fl-sandy) · [Sea-level rise](unit5-flooding.qmd#fl-rgss) · [Designing solutions for worsening floods](unit5-flooding.qmd#fl-design) · [Your PTO page: Flooding](unit5-flooding.qmd#fl-pt)
:::

::: {.u5c-fix}
**📌 Packet note:** a few lesson materials say "spring tides" happen in spring, or that the Moon is closest "once a year." **Spring tides happen twice every month** (at new and full moon), and the Moon passes perigee about **every 27.5 days**. Also, a full moon didn't *cause* Sandy. The Moon set the **starting water level**; the storm made the **surge**.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!): Flooding PTO, questions 1 and 6

**Q1. What caused the flooding in Hurricane Sandy?** On October 29, 2012, the Moon was full, so the Sun, Earth and Moon were nearly in line and their pulls added up: a **spring tide**. Sandy's winds and low pressure pushed a **storm surge** of about 9.3 ft toward New York Harbor, arriving near the evening high tide. Storm tide = tide + surge, so the water at The Battery hit a record 14.06 ft above MLLW. Sea-level rise means every tide now starts higher than in the past.

**Q6. Design element → how it addresses the mechanism (sample):**

::: {.u5c-scroll}
| Design element | How it addresses the problem and connects to the science |
|---|---|
| Berm built higher than Sandy's storm tide, plus room for sea-level rise | Storm tide = tide + surge. The height comes from the worst case (spring tide + surge) plus future sea-level rise. |
| Flood gates closed using tide and surge forecasts | Tides are predictable from Sun-Moon positions. Close the gates before king tides and forecast surges. |
| Wetland edge | Slows waves and absorbs some of the surge before it reaches the berm. |
:::
:::

### 📏 Try it: will your barrier hold? (a model)

Coastal engineers start with the question: **how high could the water get?** Pick a tide and a storm surge, add some future **sea-level rise**, then set the height of your barrier. All heights are in **feet above MLLW** at The Battery, the same scale NOAA uses.

::: {.u5c-model-note}
**This is a simple add-up model, not a real engineering calculation.** The tide and surge values are **real NOAA measurements and predictions**, but real surges and tides interact, waves add more height, and the ground behind a real barrier sits at different heights. The sea-level rise slider is a **what-if**.
:::

:::

(The same data are on the <a href="unit5-opening.html#u5o-text-2">Unit Opening</a> page.)</p>

### Will storms be more frequent and more intense?

Here is what the evidence from this unit says. Notice that some parts are **strong** and some are **uncertain**.

::: {.u5c-scroll}
| Evidence from the unit | What it suggests for the future | How sure? |
|---|---|---|
| Billion-dollar winter storms, hurricanes and floods: **16** in the 1980s, **37** in the 2010s (NOAA) | Costly storms have become more common. Costs also depend on how many people and buildings are in harm's way. | Strong for the past |
| Warm air holds about **7% more water vapor per 1 °C** of warming (IPCC); ocean heat content is rising ([Water](unit5-water.qmd#wt-ohc)) | Storms can carry and drop **more water**. | Strong for precipitation |
| Global sea level up **8–9 in since 1880**; high-tide flooding **300% to more than 900%** more frequent than 50 years ago (NOAA Climate.gov) | Every tide and every surge **starts higher**, so floods reach farther. | Strong for coastal flooding |
| Wind belts and storm paths ([Wind](unit5-wind.qmd#wd-wind-belts)) | Storms will keep following **predictable paths**. This unit didn't study how storm winds will change. | Uncertain for wind |
:::

::: {.u5c-student-task}
### ✏️ In class: Anchor Phenomenon table discussion

With your table, generate **more ideas about designing solutions** to the problem of storm damage in the United States:

- Which **subproblem** (wind, precipitation or flooding) causes the most damage where **you** live?
- What **criteria** must a solution meet? Try to make at least one **measurable**.
- What **constraints** will it have to work within (money, space, time, materials, community approval)?
- If storms get wetter and seas keep rising, how should a solution built **today** plan for the **future**?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

- **Where you live matters.** NYC's billion-dollar costs come mostly from **hurricanes**, and Sandy showed that **coastal flooding** does the biggest damage here. New York also has the **2nd-highest winter storm costs** of any state (NOAA).
- **Strong criteria are measurable and prioritized**, for example: "keeps the subway dry during a storm tide as high as Sandy's, plus 1 ft for sea-level rise," or "costs less than the damage it prevents."
- **Constraints** include budget, limited space between the water and buildings, construction time, keeping shipping and drainage open, and **community approval**.
- **Plan for the future.** Since warmer air carries more water and sea level keeps rising, a solution built today should be designed for **bigger water levels than the past**, not just the last storm.
:::

# Final Performance Task {#u5c-final}

::: {.u5c-evaluate-box}
## 🛠️ How can we design solutions that address the mechanisms and impacts of storm damage in the United States?

**The future of storms is uncertain**, but we have good reason to believe that extremely damaging storms will keep happening, and that **better solutions are needed**.

**Your task (on your own):** break the big problem of "storm damage" into **subproblems**, choose one, and **design a solution** to it that also helps with the problem overall. Your design must connect to the **mechanism** of how storms form, meet your **criteria and constraints**, and weigh **costs and benefits**.
:::

## Creating the Final Design {#u5c-design}

From your PTO, your design should:

- **Achieve your goal** (solve the problem).
- Take into consideration **all of the constraints and criteria** that have been identified.
- Be **high-leverage**: address many parts of the problem at once.
- **Align the science concepts** you have learned with any research you may have done.
- Demonstrate how **different components in the system interact**.
- Include **at least five key design elements**. A design element is something you would **change, add or take away** from the system to address the problem.

::: {.u5c-fix}
**📌 Rubric note:** the PTO says to design for **one** subproblem, but the Final Design Rubric's top level asks for elements that address **at least two subproblems**. Both work together: choose **one main subproblem**, then pick **high-leverage** design elements that also help with a second subproblem (for example, a raised, planted waterfront park that blocks storm surge **and** soaks up heavy rain). Your choice can also have its own smaller parts, like **tide timing**, **surge** and **sea-level rise** inside flooding.
:::

### Step 2: Draw your final design (the system model)

Your **Final Design** is a **drawn or 3D model**. Make it on paper (or build it), then photograph it if your teacher asks. To reach **Proficient** on the rubric, your model should include:

- The **components of the system that cause the weather phenomenon** (for flooding: Sun, Moon, tides, storm surge, sea level; for wind: air masses, high and low pressure, wind belts; for precipitation: warm ocean, moist air, front, cold air).
- The **points where your solution steps in**, with each design element **labeled**.
- **Clear annotations**, with arrows showing how **at least two components affect each other**.

  const updateStatus = () => {
    const named = elements.filter(e => (e.name || "").trim()).length;
    const lever = elements.filter(e => (e.name || "").trim() && Array.isArray(e.subs) && e.subs.length >= 2).length;
    const withMech = elements.filter(e => (e.name || "").trim() && (e.mech || "").trim()).length;
    const rDone = rFields.filter(f => rEls[f.id] && rEls[f.id].value.trim().length > 20).length;
    status.innerHTML = `<b>Design elements named:</b> ${named} ${named >= 5 ? "✅" : "(need at least 5)"}<br>` +
      `<b>High-leverage elements</b> (help 2 or more subproblems): ${lever}<br>` +
      `<b>Elements linked to a mechanism:</b> ${withMech}<br>` +
      `<b>Rationale parts started:</b> ${rDone} / 5`;
  };
  const drawList = () => {
    list.replaceChildren();
    elements.forEach((e, i) => {
      const card = mk("div", "background:#fff;border:1px solid #cbd5e1;border-left:6px solid #0284c7;border-radius:10px;padding:10px 12px;margin:10px 0;color:#0f172a;");
      card.appendChild(mk("div", "font-weight:800;color:#0f172a;", `Design element ${i + 1}`));
      const nameId = `u5c-el-${i}-name`;
      const nl = mk("label", null, "What is it?"); nl.className = "u5c-lbl"; nl.htmlFor = nameId;
      const name = document.createElement("input"); name.type = "text"; name.className = "u5c-input"; name.id = nameId; name.value = e.name || "";
      name.placeholder = "e.g., deployable flood gates at subway entrances";
      name.oninput = () => { e.name = name.value; save(); };
      const actId = `u5c-el-${i}-act`;
      const al = mk("label", null, "Do you add, change or take away something?"); al.className = "u5c-lbl"; al.htmlFor = actId;
      const act = document.createElement("select"); act.className = "u5c-select"; act.id = actId;
      actions.forEach(o => { const op = document.createElement("option"); op.textContent = o; act.appendChild(op); });
      act.value = e.act || "Add";
      act.onchange = () => { e.act = act.value; save(); };
      const sg = mk("fieldset", "border:none;padding:0;margin:8px 0 0;");
      sg.appendChild(mk("legend", "font-weight:700;color:#0f172a;", "Which subproblems does it help?"));
      const sRow = mk("div", "display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:6px;");
      subsList.forEach(s => {
        const l = mk("label", "display:inline-flex;align-items:center;gap:6px;min-height:44px;padding:4px 10px;border:1px solid #cbd5e1;border-radius:20px;cursor:pointer;color:#0f172a;");
        const cb = document.createElement("input"); cb.type = "checkbox"; cb.style.cssText = "width:20px;height:20px;";
        cb.checked = Array.isArray(e.subs) && e.subs.includes(s);
        cb.onchange = () => { const cur = new Set(e.subs || []); cb.checked ? cur.add(s) : cur.delete(s); e.subs = [...cur]; save(); };
        l.append(cb, document.createTextNode(s));
        sRow.appendChild(l);
      });
      sg.appendChild(sRow);
      const ta = (key, label, ph) => {
        const id = `u5c-el-${i}-${key}`;
        const l = mk("label", null, label); l.className = "u5c-lbl"; l.htmlFor = id;
        const t = document.createElement("textarea"); t.className = "u5c-textarea"; t.style.minHeight = "56px"; t.id = id; t.value = e[key] || ""; t.placeholder = ph;
        t.oninput = () => { e[key] = t.value; save(); };
        return [l, t];
      };
      card.append(nl, name, al, act, sg,
        ...ta("mech", "Mechanism it acts on (the science)", "e.g., storm tide = tide + surge; gates close before king tides"),
        ...ta("ben", "Benefit", ""),
        ...ta("cost", "Cost or unintended consequence", ""));
      if (elements.length > 5) {
        const rm = mk("button", null, "Remove this element"); rm.type = "button"; rm.className = "u5c-btn u5c-btn-grey";
        rm.onclick = () => { elements.splice(i, 1); save(); drawList(); };
        card.appendChild(rm);
      }
      list.appendChild(card);
    });
  };
  box.appendChild(list);
  const add = mk("button", null, "➕ Add another design element"); add.type = "button"; add.className = "u5c-btn";
  add.onclick = () => { if (elements.length < 10) { elements.push({}); save(); drawList(); } };
  box.appendChild(add);
  const rHead = mk("div", "font-weight:800;font-size:1.05em;margin:18px 0 4px;color:#0f172a;", "✍️ Design Rationale");
  rHead.id = "u5c-rationale-planner";
  box.appendChild(rHead);
  rFields.forEach(f => {
    const id = `u5c-pl-${f.id}`;
    const lab = mk("label", null, f.label); lab.className = "u5c-lbl"; lab.htmlFor = id;
    const t = document.createElement("textarea"); t.className = "u5c-textarea"; t.id = id; t.value = saved[f.id] || "";
    rEls[f.id] = t;
    box.append(lab, t);
  });
  box.appendChild(status);
  const msg = mk("span", "font-size:.88em;color:#0f172a;");
  msg.setAttribute("aria-live", "polite");
  const outline = () => {
    const d = read();
    const els = elements.map((e, i) => `Design element ${i + 1}: ${e.name || "(blank)"} [${e.act || "Add"}]\n  Helps: ${(e.subs || []).join(", ") || "(none checked)"}\n  Mechanism: ${e.mech || ""}\n  Benefit: ${e.ben || ""}\n  Cost: ${e.cost || ""}`).join("\n\n");
    return `FINAL DESIGN TASK\n\nMain subproblem: ${d.sub}\nPlace: ${d.place}\n\nBreaking down storm damage:\n${d.breakdown}\n\nCriteria (most important first):\n${d.criteria}\n\nConstraints and limitations:\n${d.constraints}\n\n${els}\n\nDESIGN RATIONALE\n` + rFields.map(f => `\n${f.label}\n${d[f.id] || ""}`).join("\n");
  };
  const copy = mk("button", null, "📋 Copy my whole design"); copy.type = "button"; copy.className = "u5c-btn";
  copy.onclick = async () => {
    const text = outline();
    try { await navigator.clipboard.writeText(text); msg.textContent = "Copied! Paste it into your notes or PTO."; }
    catch (e) { pre.textContent = text; pre.style.display = "block"; msg.textContent = "Copy isn't available here. Select the text below and copy it."; }
  };
  const prev = mk("button", null, "👀 Preview"); prev.type = "button"; prev.className = "u5c-btn";
  const pre = mk("div", "display:none;white-space:pre-wrap;background:#fff;border:1px solid #cbd5e1;border-radius:8px;padding:10px;margin-top:8px;font-size:.88em;color:#0f172a;");
  prev.onclick = () => { pre.textContent = outline(); pre.style.display = "block"; };
  const clear = mk("button", null, "🗑️ Clear"); clear.type = "button"; clear.className = "u5c-btn u5c-btn-grey";
  clear.onclick = () => {
    if (!confirm("Clear your whole design plan?")) return;
    elements = Array.from({length: 5}, () => ({}));
    top.forEach(f => fields[f.id].value = f.type === "select" ? f.opts[0] : "");
    rFields.forEach(f => rEls[f.id].value = "");
    try { localStorage.removeItem(KEY); } catch (e) {}
    pre.style.display = "none"; drawList(); updateStatus(); msg.textContent = "Cleared.";
  };
  const btnRow = mk("div");
  btnRow.append(prev, copy, clear, msg);
  box.append(btnRow, pre);
  box.addEventListener("input", ev => { if (ev.target.closest && !ev.target.id.startsWith("u5c-el-")) save(); });
  box.addEventListener("change", ev => { if (ev.target.tagName === "SELECT" && ev.target.id.startsWith("u5c-pl-")) save(); });
  drawList();
  updateStatus();
  return box;
}
```

## Design Rationale {#u5c-rationale}

Write a **rationale** that explains how **at least three** of your design elements address the problem and the subproblems you identified this unit. Your PTO asks for five parts (the planner above has a box for each):

1. A description of the **overall problem**, including relevant **science concepts**.
2. A description of **at least one subproblem**, including relevant science concepts.
3. How the **design elements address the subproblems**, including the **mechanism** each one acts on.
4. How **at least one design element** addresses your **criteria and constraints**.
5. How the design **overall balances benefits with costs**.

::: {.u5c-key-idea}
### 🧠 Two big ideas the rubric looks for

- **Patterns:** storms follow **predictable paths**, precipitation follows **wet and dry latitudes and fronts**, and tides follow the **Moon's phases and distance**. Say how a pattern shaped **where** or **when** your solution works.
- **Influence of technology on society:** every new technology can affect people and the environment, **including in ways nobody planned**. Name at least one **unintended consequence** of your design (for example, a sea wall that protects one block can send water to the next).
:::

**Sentence starters:**

- "Storm damage is a problem because ___. One subproblem is ___, which happens because ___."
- "Design element ___ acts on the mechanism by ___, **because** ___."
- "My most important criterion is ___. Element ___ meets it **because** ___. One constraint is ___, so I ___."
- "A pattern I used is ___, which means my solution ___."
- "The benefits (___) are worth the costs (___) **because** ___. One unintended consequence could be ___."

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!): a sample design for a NYC waterfront neighborhood

**Main subproblem:** coastal flooding. **High-leverage idea:** most elements also help with heavy rain or wind.

::: {.u5c-scroll}
| # | Design element | Subproblems it helps | Mechanism it acts on | Benefit | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Add** a raised waterfront park with a berm, built higher than Sandy's storm tide plus room for sea-level rise | Flooding, people | Storm tide = tide + surge, starting from a rising sea | Blocks surge; park for everyday use | Expensive, takes years, can push water to neighbors |
| 2 | **Add** flood gates at subway entrances, closed using tide and surge forecasts | Flooding, people | Tides are predictable from Sun-Moon positions | Protects transit during king tides and surges | Must be staffed and maintained |
| 3 | **Change** the shoreline edge to a planted wetland | Flooding, precipitation | Absorbs wave energy and some surge; soaks up rain | Natural, habitat for wildlife | Needs space; protects more slowly |
| 4 | **Change** power lines near the shore to buried, flood-proofed lines | Wind, flooding | Wind and falling trees knock down overhead lines | Fewer outages in high winds | Costs more; harder to repair |
| 5 | **Add** a storm warning plan that uses forecasts of storm paths and king tides | Wind, precipitation, flooding, people | Storms follow the westerlies; tides are predictable | People prepare and evacuate early | Only works if people get the warning and can act |
:::

**Rationale (part 5, sample):** The berm and wetland together protect against a Sandy-sized storm tide, which meets my top criterion (keep homes and the subway dry). They cost a lot and take years, but the damage from one Sandy-sized storm is far greater. One **unintended consequence** is that water blocked here could flood the next neighborhood, so the plan needs to be coordinated along the whole shoreline.
:::

## Final Design Rubric {#u5c-rubric}

This is the **Final Design Rubric** from your Unit Closing handout. Your teacher will use it to score your design.

::: {.u5c-scroll}
| Component | Level 1: Beginning | Level 2: Developing | Level 3: Advancing | Level 4: Proficient |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Representing the System** | 3D or drawn model with no annotations, labels or system components | Annotations, labels and/or system components are inaccurate or missing | Annotations and labels are mostly clear; most system components are shown | Annotations and labels are clear; **all major components** are shown, and it's clear how **at least 2 components are interrelated** |
| **Design Elements** | Fewer than 5 elements, but at least 1 addresses a subproblem and/or some criteria or constraints | Fewer than 5 elements; at least 2 address 1 or more subproblems and some criteria or constraints | **5** elements; most address at least 2 subproblems and most criteria and constraints | **At least 5** elements; **all** address at least 2 subproblems and take into account **all** criteria and constraints |
| **Design Rationale** | Restates evidence; no science concepts or crosscutting concepts | Science concepts are inappropriate or don't link evidence to the claim; crosscutting concepts not addressed | Some science concepts link evidence to the claim but some are missing; crosscutting concepts addressed but not enough | Clear rationale for **at least 3** design elements, with **all** the science concepts, how **all** criteria and constraints shaped the elements, and how **patterns** and **the influence of technology on society** informed the design |
:::

<p class="u5c-note">"Not Evident" means the component is missing. The rubric notes that the system's components depend on your subproblem, but should include what <b>generates the weather phenomenon</b> and the points where <b>your solution steps in</b>.</p>

::: {.u5c-evaluate-box}
### ✅ Proficient checklist

Tap each item when your design includes it.
:::

  const bar = html`<div style="background:#e2e8f0;border-radius:20px;height:14px;overflow:hidden;margin:6px 0 4px;"><div style="background:linear-gradient(90deg,#0284c7,#ad1457);height:100%;width:0%;transition:width .3s;"></div></div>`;
  box.append(label, bar);
  const update = () => {
    const n = box.querySelectorAll("input:checked").length;
    bar.firstChild.style.width = `${100 * n / total}%`;
    label.textContent = n === total ? `🎉 ${n} of ${total}: your design meets every Proficient item!` : `${n} of ${total} Proficient items included`;
  };
  groups.forEach(g => {
    const h = document.createElement("div");
    h.style.cssText = "font-weight:800;margin:14px 0 4px;color:#075985;";
    h.textContent = g.title;
    box.appendChild(h);
    g.items.forEach(it => {
      const lab = document.createElement("label");
      lab.style.cssText = "display:flex;gap:10px;align-items:flex-start;padding:8px 6px;min-height:44px;border-bottom:1px solid #e2e8f0;cursor:pointer;color:#0f172a;";
      const cb = document.createElement("input");
      cb.type = "checkbox";
      cb.style.cssText = "width:22px;height:22px;flex:0 0 22px;margin-top:2px;";
      cb.onchange = update;
      const sp = document.createElement("span");
      sp.textContent = it;
      lab.append(cb, sp);
      box.appendChild(lab);
    });
  });
  update();
  return box;
}

# Unit Summary {#u5c-summary}

::: {.u5c-scroll}
| Big idea | What you figured out |
|---|---|
| **The problem** | Storms cost the US billions of dollars every year and harm people's lives. From 1980 to 2024, billion-dollar hurricanes, floods and winter storms cost about **$1.85 trillion** (NOAA). |
| **Breaking it down** | Engineers split a big problem into **subproblems**: strong **winds**, heavy **precipitation** and coastal **flooding**. Each has a different **mechanism**. |
| **Wind** | **Uneven heating** → density and **pressure** differences → air flows **from high to low**. Wind belts and the **Coriolis effect** steer storms; a big pressure difference over a short distance makes strong wind. |
| **Water** | Warm, moist air is **lifted at fronts**, cools and **condenses** into rain or snow. Warmer air holds more water vapor, so storms can drop more. |
| **Flooding** | **Storm tide = tide + surge.** Spring tides (new and full moon) and king tides (plus perigee) raise the starting level; sea-level rise raises it further. |
| **Engineering** | Good solutions meet **criteria**, work within **constraints**, accept reasonable **tradeoffs**, and are built from **design elements** that act on the **mechanism**. |
| **Patterns and society** | Predictable patterns (storm paths, tides) tell us **where and when** to act. Every technology can have **unintended consequences**, so we weigh **costs and benefits**. |
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 📚 Data and sources on this page

- **Billion-dollar disasters:** NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, [U.S. Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/billions/), 1980–2024 (2024 dollars).
- **Tides and storm tides at The Battery, NY (station 8518750):** NOAA CO-OPS [Tides & Currents](https://tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov/stationhome.html?id=8518750): verified water levels, tide predictions and datums.
- **Sea-level rise and high-tide flooding:** NOAA Climate.gov, [Climate Change: Global Sea Level](https://www.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/climate-change-global-sea-level).
- **Winter Storm Jonas:** National Weather Service New York (OKX) storm summary; NOAA Central Park daily records and 1991–2020 normals.
- **Hurricane Helene:** National Hurricane Center, Tropical Cyclone Report AL092024.
- **Water vapor and temperature:** IPCC AR6 Working Group I.
- **Wind turbines:** U.S. Department of Energy, [Wind Turbines in Extreme Weather: Solutions for Hurricane Resiliency](https://www.energy.gov/cmei/systems/articles/wind-turbines-extreme-weather-solutions-hurricane-resiliency) (2018).
- **Geoengineering figures:** as cited in the Water lesson's text (Columbia Climate School 2024; NOAA Research 2021; Hlywiak & Nolan 2022).
- **Curriculum:** New Visions for Public Schools, Earth and Space Science Unit 5, *Extreme Weather Coming to a Place Near You?* (SY 26-27), Performance Task Organizer and Unit Closing materials, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.
:::
